source.title: Generalization error of random feature and kernel methods: hypercontractivity and kernel matrix concentration
source.authors: Song Mei; Theodor Misiakiewicz; A. Montanari

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a theoretical characterization and a simulation of test error across feature-count and sample-size regimes. It tests a related double-descent pattern in random-feature and kernel methods, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: Findings cited from other work are not rows. Figure 1 reports an aggregate over 10 realizations; plotted values are not numerically tabulated. Theorems 1 and 2 also report asymptotic risk characterizations.
record.test_reason: The study uses its own simulation and theorems on random-features ridge regression, a non-deep model class, and reports test risk across N and n around the interpolation threshold N≈n. Its Figure 1 heatmap shows a risk peak at N≈n and lower risk on either side, which bears on V4 and, through the N↔n symmetry, on V3. It is not one of the original sources. The method differs from the originals (polynomial-scaling asymptotics plus a d = 50 sphere simulation), hence T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the smaller of n and N governs RFRR test risk, which shows a large peak at N≈n and symmetry in N and n. For N ≥ n^(1+δ) the risk matches KRR and further increasing N gives no significant change. They also conclude that min-norm interpolation (λ→0) is optimal among kernel methods in the overparametrized regime.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random-feature ridge regression and kernel ridge regression under spectral and concentration assumptions, with an analytical asymptotic characterization and a d = 50 sphere simulation; it does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The Figure 1 simulation fixes a noiseless target, shifted ReLU activation, and minimum-norm interpolation; the paper does not report a systematic sensitivity sweep over these choices.

fits_no_version.finding: In the overparametrized polynomial regime, every λ in [0, λ*] gives the same risk. No kernel method beats the projection risk (Theorem 3), so min-norm interpolation is optimal among kernel methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Far from the interpolation threshold, overparametrized min-norm interpolators are optimal and ridge tuning gives no gain.

fits_no_version.finding: The N≈n risk peak appears with zero label noise (σε = 0).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak in random-features regression occurs even without label noise; variance from the random features suffices.

record.problems: The illustrative simulation uses d = 50, one stated target, zero noise, one activation, and minimum-norm interpolation, and averages 10 realizations without reporting uncertainty bars or tabulated risk values. The theorems apply under stated asymptotic assumptions and do not establish the deep-network or epoch-wise versions.

untested.parts: No deep networks. Random-features models are only a stylized proxy for lazy-regime networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested for predicting peak location across size, epoch and sample axes.

The simulation uses zero label noise only, with no noise sweep. Multiple peaks are not studied. Whether tuned ridge removes the N≈n peak is not tested; the theorems cover only the regimes away from N≈n.
No re-counting of complexity with an effective-parameter measure.

missing.what: Comparison across Theorem 1(a) and 1(b) at fixed n: overparametrized risk ||P>m f||² is at most the risk of any underparametrized N (||P>M f||² with M ≤ m). Overparametrized RFRR therefore beats or matches all underparametrized sizes.
missing.locator: Section 1.2, 'Effects of overparametrization' and 'Optimal overparametrization'; Theorem 1

missing.what: Lower bound for general kernel methods (Theorem 3), showing min-norm interpolators are optimal in the N ≫ n regime.

record.verdict_notes: The N≈n peak itself is attributed to the earlier proportional-regime work [HMRT19, MM19]; this paper's contribution is the polynomial-regime characterization away from the peak. The V3 and V4 support rests on a figure described only in words: 10 realizations, no error bars, no tabulated values.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies random-feature ridge regression and kernel methods, not deep networks.
No test-error sweep over training epochs or training time.
The more-data effect is illustrated in the random-feature setting and at the reported simulation setting; no deep-network setting is tested.
The results concern random-feature and kernel methods under the stated assumptions and a sphere simulation, not a broad empirical survey of model classes.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts the peak location across size, epochs, and sample-size axes.
The simulation uses no noise; there is no systematic test of noise-driven or multiple peaks, or of peak disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
The paper does not re-count parameters using an effective-parameter measure or show that the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: random features ridge regression (RFRR)
rows.size_stated: d = 50; number of neurons N varied
rows.operation_detail: Sweep the number of neurons N and sample size n for minimum-norm interpolation and report average test risk.

conditions.value: uniform distribution on the sphere S^{d−1}(√d)

rows.note: The text describes a large risk peak at N≈n and symmetry around that line. The heatmap averages over 10 realizations; no numerical test-error values are given.
rows.check: Figure-only. The state rests on the authors' text: 'blow-up at the interpolation threshold N ≈ n' and 'symmetry around this line'. The symmetry implies that at fixed N, raising n toward N raises risk (V3); no risk values are tabulated.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.4, Eq. (35), Figure 1 caption and accompanying discussion, pp. 16–17.

rows.subject: random features ridge regression (RFRR)
rows.size_stated: N and n grow with d; N(d) ≥ d^δ n(d) for some δ > 0
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 1(a) characterizes test risk in the overparametrized regime.

conditions.value: N(d) ≥ d^δ n(d) for some δ > 0

rows.measure: test error RRF(fd, X, Θ, λ)
rows.value: |RRF(fd, X, Θ, λ) − ||P>m fd||²L2| ≤ ε · (||fd||²L2 + ||P>m fd||²L2+η + σε²), with high probability
rows.uncertainty: The stated high-probability bound holds for fixed η > 0 and ε > 0.
rows.note: This gives an asymptotic risk characterization far into the overparametrized regime, not a direct measurement of the fall-rise-fall curve across the interpolation point.
rows.check: Theorem 1(a) shows that for N ≥ d^δ·n the risk is about ||P>m f||², insensitive to N and equal to the KRR limit. So beyond the peak the second descent levels off rather than improving further. The row alone cannot show the peak itself.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for V4. Theorem 1(a) establishes an asymptotic projection-error characterization for N(d) ≥ d^δ n(d), under Assumptions 1–2; it does not characterize the transition through N≈n or establish an incomplete second descent.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.3, Theorem 1(a), Eq. (21), and following discussion, pp. 13–14.
source_check.problem: A characterization confined to the far-overparametrized regime cannot establish that the double-descent effect is partial.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is the January 2021 arXiv v1. The authors' optimality and KRR-equivalence conclusions are asymptotic and assumption-dependent; the interpolation-threshold peak is illustrated numerically, outside the separated regimes of Theorem 1.

statements.correction: Figure 1: d=50; fourth-order polynomial target; shifted ReLU; σε=0; λ=0+; mean test error over 10 realizations; peak near N≈n; approximate symmetry under exchanging N and n. No reported empirical error bars or confidence intervals. Theorems 1–2: high-probability risk bounds under stated assumptions.
statements.problem: The noiseless polynomial-target experiment and peak near n=N are supported. Empirical uncertainty for that experiment is not quantified: averaging realizations does not provide an uncertainty estimate. High-probability theorem bounds concern a separate asymptotic characterization.
